source1: Kathleen D. Morrison (University of Chicago), Early Historic Landscapes of the Tungabhadra Corridor, project page, University of Chicago Paleoecology Laboratory - http://paleoecology.uchicago.edu/ehltc/
source2: e-PG Pathshala (INFLIBNET/UGC), Pre and Protohistoric Cultures of India, ch. 32 'Iron Age - Early Historic Transition in South India' - https://ebooks.inflibnet.ac.in/icp02/chapter/iron-age-early-historic-transition-in-south-india/
notes: Archaeological phase, no recorded central authority. Megalith-building and settlement continued into the Early Historic; Ashokan minor rock edicts (c. 260 BCE) show Mauryan control of key Karnataka towns, which the S4 rule keeps out of T2.

source1: V.N. Prabhakar, 'Protohistory of India and Pakistan VI: Post Harappan Cultures', Pre and Protohistoric Cultures of India ch. 24, e-PG Pathshala (INFLIBNET/UGC) - https://ebooks.inflibnet.ac.in/icp02/chapter/protohistory-of-india-and-pakistan-vi-post-harappan-cultures/
source2: Gregory L. Possehl, 'The transformation of the Indus Civilization', Journal of World Prehistory 11(4), 1997 - https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF02220556
notes: Archaeological phase. Nausharo stayed occupied through the Mature Harappan; its final Indus phase links to the Mehrgarh VIII complex. Central Asian elements (Sibri) could suggest newcomers, so T4 is not excluded. Sources do not address 2100 BCE itself.

source1: Department of Asian Art, 'Jomon Culture (ca. 10,500-ca. 300 B.C.)', Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, Metropolitan Museum of Art, 2002 - https://www.metmuseum.org/toah/hd/jomo/hd_jomo.htm
source2: T.A. Jinam, H. Kanzawa-Kiriyama & N. Saitou, 'Human genetic diversity in the Japanese Archipelago: dual structure and beyond', Genes & Genetic Systems 90(3), 2015 - https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/ggs/90/3/90_147/_article
notes: Archaeological phase. Late to Final Jomon was a continuous hunter-gatherer Jomon culture; population moved and fell as the climate cooled. Continental migrants arrive only with Yayoi, after c. 1000 BCE. Britannica's uncalibrated scheme dates Late Jomon c. 1500-1000 BCE.

successor: Bamana (Segou) kingdom of Biton Mamari Kulibali
source1: Encyclopaedia Britannica Editors, 'Bambara states', Encyclopaedia Britannica - https://www.britannica.com/place/Bambara-states
source2: Alexander Ives Bortolot, 'The Bamana Segou State', Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, Metropolitan Museum of Art, 2003 - https://www.metmuseum.org/essays/the-bamana-segou-state
notes: Kaladian Kulibali's Segou state (c.1652-82) disintegrated after his death (Britannica); Biton Kulibali's ton army displaced the elders and founded a new state c.1712 (Met). No external conquest. If P is taken to end in 1712, T1c is the alternative.

source1: D.L. Holmes & R.F. Friedman, 'Survey and Test Excavations in the Badari Region, Egypt', Proceedings of the Prehistoric Society 60, 1994 - https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/proceedings-of-the-prehistoric-society/article/abs/survey-and-test-excavations-in-the-badari-region-egypt/3A177F54A6FA9C0C5DAD45F3BE828886
source2: Encyclopaedia Britannica Editors, 'Amratian culture', Encyclopaedia Britannica - https://www.britannica.com/topic/Amratian-culture
notes: Archaeological phase. The Hemamieh pottery sequence runs unbroken from Badarian through Gerzean, and Badarian traits may persist locally into Amratian times; Britannica calls Amratian life similar to Badarian. Badarian C14 dates c.4400-4000 BC; end date uncertain.

successor: Early Monte Alban I (Monte Alban polity)
source1: Kent V. Flannery & Joyce Marcus (project contacts), 'Origins of the State', Archaeological Research in Oaxaca, University of Michigan Museum of Anthropological Archaeology - https://sites.lsa.umich.edu/oaxaca-archaeology/origins-of-the-state/
source2: Charles S. Spencer, 'Modeling (and Measuring) Expansionism and Resistance: State Formation in Ancient Oaxaca, Mexico', History & Mathematics almanac - https://sociostudies.org/almanac/articles/modeling_expansionism_and_resistance_state_formation_in_ancient_oaxaca_mexico
notes: About 2,000 people from San Jose Mogote and its satellites founded Monte Alban c.500 BC (UMMAA; Spencer): the chiefly elite relocated, with no conquest. Blanton et al. stress a cooperative founding (possible T6). Rosario raids were between chiefdoms.
